somm-v1.prompt: You are tasting a young Barolo ahead of a big game supper. The wine is very astringent and you wonder whether it suits the dishes. What happens chemically when a tannic wine meets the protein in game meat?
options: The tannins dissolve and disappear from the experience
The tannins bind to the proteins in the meat — the astringency drops and the wine feels softer
The tannins markedly strengthen the meat's umami
The protein blocks every taste impression from the wine
somm-v1.explanation: Tannin binding is the core: tannins react with proteins and bind to them. The meat 'takes care of' the tannin — the astringency softens and the wine opens up. Herdenstam describes how this analysis happens during the twelve seconds in the mouth, in the actual situation.

somm-v2.prompt: A guest at Herrgårdsköket orders a full-bodied Alsace Riesling with their foie gras. Your colleague questions the choice: 'Riesling and foie gras? That can't work.' Which scientific reasoning defends the pairing best?
options: Riesling's high acidity cuts through the richness of the foie gras and cleanses the palate, while any residual sugar balances the flavour of the liver
Riesling's petrol notes directly complement the liver aroma
Foie gras is always better with red wine, whatever the region
Riesling's high alcohol balances the weight of the fat
somm-v2.explanation: Palate cleansing: high acidity cuts through fat and restores the palate's sensitivity. Residual sugar in a demi-sec Riesling also balances the intensity of the liver. Harrington's pyramid: the basic-taste level (acid against fat) is resolved before you address flavours.

somm-v3.prompt: You are at a wine fair and will taste through 80 wines in one day. You start with light whites and finish with powerful reds. Halfway through you notice that your palate no longer responds as distinctly. What is the main physiological reason your judgement gets worse during a long tasting session?
options: The room temperature rises and harms the wine's volatile compounds
Hunger affects the brain's signalling substances
You forget the first wines
Alcohol, tannins and high taste intensity tire the taste receptors — palate fatigue — so the distinctions blur
somm-v3.explanation: Herdenstam describes this precisely from his working life: the alcohol numbs, the tannic grip lingers, and the intensity of powerful wines makes it hard to reset the palate for subtle ones. The remedy is water, neutral food and the right tasting order.

somm-v4.prompt: You are training new staff at Lärkan. A new colleague asks why you always start a tasting with sight, then smell, then taste — in that order. Why is the WSET SAT order (Appearance → Nose → Palate → Conclusions) designed that way?
options: Appearance is always the most important part of judging quality
It is an old tradition with no scientific basis
The order is arbitrary — every order gives the same result
The structure makes sure each sense is judged without being swayed by the next: what you see does not colour the nose, the nose does not colour the palate
somm-v4.explanation: WSET SAT is designed to reduce bias. Herdenstam stresses that sensory analysis needs a system to capture what can be measured — and reminds us that this analytical method must be complemented by the creative grip to capture the whole.

somm-v5.prompt: Nocturne is building a new wine list focused on sustainability. You are to argue to the owner why biodynamic farming (Demeter) is a stronger choice than ordinary organic certification. Which argument is the most soundly based?
options: Biodynamic farming always produces better wine
Biodynamic farming (Demeter) treats the vineyard as a closed ecosystem with biodiversity and no synthetic inputs, giving resilience and credibility beyond what organic certification requires
Demeter certification is cheaper than organic certification
Biodynamic farming removes all climate impact
somm-v5.explanation: Demeter requires the whole farm to be treated as a living system, with biodiversity and farming adapted to a lunar calendar. It goes further than EU organic certification, which allows certain inputs. For a sustainability profile, Demeter gives the strongest case to guests and auditors.

somm-v6.prompt: A guest at Ekbacken asks why a wine that smells of cherries from the bottle starts to taste of butter and toast once it is in the mouth. What is the scientific explanation for the difference between retronasal and orthonasal aroma?
options: Orthonasal smell comes in through the nose from outside; retronasal smell is the aromas rising through the throat as we chew, and it makes up as much as 80 % of what we call 'taste'
The warmth of the mouth breaks cherry aromas down into butter compounds
The guest's taste memory is faulty
The shape of the glass changes the aromas chemically
somm-v6.explanation: Herdenstam stresses retronasal smell as central to the taster's work: 'what we call taste is largely a smell experienced the back way'. Pairing food and drink is very much about harmonising these retronasal aromas between food and wine.

somm-v7.prompt: You are training the staff at Järnvägshotellet. You are to explain Harrington's Food & Beverage Pyramid and why you always start with the basic tastes. Why is Harrington's hierarchy (basic tastes → texture → flavours) right, both for teaching and in practice?
options: Each level must be in harmony before the next is addressed: if the basic tastes clash (high acidity against sweetness, say), no amount of flavour likeness can save the pairing
The pyramid only applies to white wines
Basic tastes are the easiest for beginners, with no other practical relevance
Flavours matter most and should always be addressed first
somm-v7.explanation: Harrington's pyramid is a hierarchy of steps, not just a classification. If the basic-taste balance fails — a dry, tannic wine with a sweet sauce, say — the experience breaks at level one and no aromas can save the pairing. Methodical tasting always starts at the bottom of the pyramid.

somm-h1.prompt: A large party dinner at Herrgårdsköket. A guest orders a young 2021 Barolo with their saddle of venison. The wine is brought up from the cellar. What do you do at once, and why?
options: Serve it with ice in the glass so the guest can choose the temperature
Serve it straight away — cold wines are always best
Decant it for 30 minutes and check that it is at 16–18 °C: young, powerful reds need oxygen to open and the right temperature to show their complexity
Warm the bottle under hot water to 22 °C
somm-h1.explanation: Herdenstam describes this as the heart of craft knowledge: knowing how to use the tool. Young Barolo has high tannins and a complex structure that needs oxygen. 16–18 °C is the ideal serving temperature for full-bodied reds; warmer dulls the fruit, colder hides the complexity and hardens the tannins.

somm-h2.prompt: A regular at Bryggan brings a bottle of 2005 Chambolle-Musigny (Premier Cru, twenty years old) and wants you to handle it professionally. What is the right way to handle an old, fine Burgundy?
options: Decant it for at least 2 hours for maximum oxygen
Stand it upright for 24 hours before service, then open and serve at once: old fine Burgundy is fragile and collapses with long decanting
Serve it straight from cellar temperature (10 °C)
Shake it gently to wake the sediment
somm-h2.explanation: Herdenstam describes how judgement built on experience — familiarity knowledge — decides such things. Old fine Burgundy has a delicate structure that can collapse if exposed to oxygen too long. Sediment is separated with a gentle decant, but exposure is kept to a minimum. The right temperature is 14–16 °C.

somm-h3.prompt: Halfway through a large wedding banquet at Ekbacken, the champagne guests start to complain that the mousse is flat and the aroma weak. You change the glasses and pour fresh wine. What was most likely the main cause, and how do you prevent it from now on?
options: Detergent residue in the glasses kills the mousse and dulls the aroma; prevent it by rinsing with wine (pour a little in, swirl, pour out) and always check the glasses before service
The dining room was too warm
The champagne was of too low a quality
The champagne stood too long and lost its fizz naturally
somm-h3.explanation: Detergent residue is the most common cause of flat champagne. Herdenstam stresses that craft knowledge means knowing how the tools work and where the faults come from. Rinsing with wine is a simple professional routine that removes the problem.

somm-h4.prompt: You are building a seven-course tasting menu at Qvarnen with seven wines. A colleague suggests opening with a powerful Amarone to 'impress straight away'. Why is it wrong to open with a powerful wine, and what is the right order?
options: The order does not matter if the wines are good
Always start with red to impress
It is not wrong — always start with the most expensive
Powerful wines tire the palate early; the right order is sparkling → light whites → full whites → light reds → full reds → dessert wines: dry to sweet, light to full
somm-h4.explanation: Herdenstam describes from his own experience at wine fairs how the palate tires and how the wrong order makes subtle wines taste flat after powerful ones. Progression is one of the craft's basic tools: sparkling wine opens the palate, dessert wines close without cloying it.

somm-h5.prompt: One of Nocturne's best-selling wines is a natural wine fined with egg white. A new regular quietly mentions that her son is allergic to egg. What do you do, and what should you already have done?
options: Take the wine off the list for now
Serve the wine — a little egg white is no problem
Tell the guest the wine is fined with egg white and offer an alternative without animal-based fining; speaking up first is the sommelier team's responsibility, not the producer's
Say all natural wines are vegan and serve it
somm-h5.explanation: Social sustainability requires inclusion and speaking up first. Herdenstam stresses that a sommelier's professional knowledge includes knowing their products in every detail. Declaring allergens is both a legal requirement and professional ethics — and it builds the guests' trust.

somm-h6.prompt: Lärkan wants to cut its wine list's climate footprint by 40 % within a year without compromising on quality. You present a plan to the owner. Which set of measures has the greatest environmental effect?
options: Switch every cork to a screwcap and serve wine colder
Favour local and Nordic producers, introduce bag-in-box for the house wines (70 % less CO₂ per litre than a glass bottle), and document the footprint of the whole list
Drop every imported wine and serve only Swedish cider
Cut portion sizes by 20 %
somm-h6.explanation: Transport and packaging dominate a wine's climate footprint. Local producers remove long transport chains. Bag-in-box gives a far smaller packaging footprint per litre. Documentation also lets you talk to guests about climate choices — a social and environmental gain in one.

somm-e1.prompt: Ekbacken is expecting a well-known food writer for a review. You are thinking about how to create a memorable experience without changing a single dish on the menu. Which approach is most in line with Herdenstam's double grip and Crichton-Fock's atmospheric influence?
options: Match the room's lighting, music and pace of service to the character of the wines — and tell the story of each wine's origin, the grower's philosophy and the vintage
Switch to more expensive wines for the reviewer
Let the reviewer choose everything without guidance
Lower the prices that evening to impress
somm-e1.explanation: Herdenstam: 'What happens, the knowledge in the doing, is what matters.' Crichton-Fock shows that every sensory impression in the room works together and sets a mood. Crossmodal correspondence (Spence) confirms that light and music change how things taste. Creating the experience means orchestrating the whole setting.

somm-e2.prompt: A regular at Bryggan always orders 'the best red wine'. Today he tells you he is turning 60. You have three to choose from: a 2015 Barolo, a 2018 Châteauneuf-du-Pape and a 2010 Pinot Noir from Burgundy. What is the creative decision here, and how do you make it?
options: Serve the wine you personally prefer
Let him choose among the three without guidance
Choose the most expensive automatically — it is always safest
Ask discreetly whether he has a link to a region, a memory or a moment in his life — then choose the wine whose story best matches his
somm-e2.explanation: Herdenstam shows that creating an experience starts with listening and reading the situation. Expectation priming: when the guest understands the story behind the wine, more layers of thought come into play and the experience deepens. A personal choice always says more than the price.

somm-e3.prompt: You are writing the menu texts for a new tasting menu at Herrgårdsköket. Your colleague suggests short, neutral descriptions: 'Riesling, Mosel, 2019'. Why does expectation priming matter here, and how do you write a better text?
options: The menu text does not affect how things taste
Neutral descriptions are always best — guests do not want to be influenced

The menu text primes the experience before the first sip: words that call up an image, a memory or a feeling change how the guest tastes the wine. Write: 'Riesling from the Mosel — steep-slope minerality, fresh citrus-blossom acidity, a scent of slate after rain'
Longer texts are always worse — keep it short
somm-e3.explanation: Expectation priming is well documented: a well-written menu text sets expectations that change how the guest experiences the taste. Herdenstam: 'In science we measure what is. In creation we make what becomes.' The menu text is a creative tool.

somm-e4.prompt: You are hosting a terroir dinner at Viken focused on the Loire Valley. One guest, a professor of cultural geography, asks how you can convey the feeling of the river and the limestone when the guest is not there. Which answer best shows Herdenstam's creative grip?
options: It is impossible — terroir can only be experienced on the spot

Tell the grower's story, put a piece of limestone on the table, show a picture of the river landscape, and let the mineral scent of the wine carry the story: analogies and sensory impressions create shared understanding without being there
Serve only wines with strong character and hope the guest understands
Explain terroir in chemical terms
somm-e4.explanation: Herdenstam: 'The link to reality becomes important, and the insight that there is not one reality but several even more so.' Analogies, sensory impressions and stories create understanding — the guest tastes with their whole cultural background. That is creating the experience in practice.

somm-e5.prompt: Nocturne is launching an alcohol-free pairing menu. A colleague is sceptical: 'No real sommelier spends time on alcohol-free — there is no prestige in it.' How do you answer, from the point of view of sustainability and creating the experience?
options: Alcohol-free options with the same care, story and presentation as the wine menu are an expression of inclusion — and a growing part of the business. A sommelier who cannot pair without alcohol has not mastered the whole craft
Offer alcohol-free only if the guest asks
Alcohol-free is always inferior and should be kept to a minimum
The colleague is right — put the wine menu first
somm-e5.explanation: Social sustainability means every guest is welcome, whatever they choose. Herdenstam shows that creative knowledge is about making an experience for the guest, not about one's own prestige. An alcohol-free pairing menu with the same story and presentation is fully worthy of the sommelier's craft.

somm-e6.prompt: During a tasting menu at Ekbacken you are playing music you chose. A guest remarks that the third wine, a powerful Syrah, seems 'sweeter and rounder' now than at the pre-tasting this evening — then you played heavier jazz, now a lighter string quartet. Which phenomenon explains the guest's experience, and what does it teach us about the sommelier's role?
options: The room temperature has changed the wine
The guest has drunk too much and misjudges
The guest is wrong — music does not change the wine

Crossmodal correspondence (Spence): high, bright music brings out perceived sweetness and elegance; heavier music brings out bitterness and astringency. The sommelier who orchestrates the setting is part of the taste
somm-e6.explanation: Spence's research (Oxford) is well documented: sound, light and setting change how we perceive taste. Herdenstam and Crichton-Fock: every sensory impression in the dining room works together. The sommelier who orchestrates the setting on purpose is practising creative knowledge at its highest level.

somm-h7.prompt: You are tasting a wine at a trade fair. After three seconds you sense that something is fundamentally wrong — the wine has a sharp, musty smell. What is most likely wrong, and what do you do?
options: The room temperature has spoiled the wine for now
The wine is too young and needs more time in bottle
The wine is probably corked (TCA, trichloroanisole): politely decline and ask for a new bottle or another wine. Cork taint ruins every aroma
The smell is typical of the grape
somm-h7.explanation: Herdenstam describes how experienced sommeliers make the call in seconds — 'even before it takes shape'. TCA cork taint is the most common fault and is recognised as a damp, mouldy, musty note. Spotting and handling it quickly is core craft.

somm-v8.prompt: A guest at Qvarnen wonders why her favourite Sauvignon Blanc tastes 'flatter' with her cream sauce than with oysters. What is the scientific explanation?
options: Sauvignon Blanc never goes with cream sauces

The cream sauce's fat and sweetness mute the wine's acidity and aromas — tart wines feel thinner against fat because the fat 'takes' the acid. Oysters instead bring out the wine's minerality and freshness
The guest is wrong — the wine tastes the same whatever the food
The cream chemically curdles the wine's proteins
somm-v8.explanation: Basic-taste interaction: acid against fat is a complex interplay in which fat softens the sharpness of the acid — but if there is too much fat, the wine feels thinner. The minerality and salt of oysters complement and strengthen the wine's own character. Harrington's pyramid, the basic-taste level.

somm-e7.prompt: A guest on her own sits quietly at Viken's window table looking out over the lake. She looks sad and orders 'a glass of white wine — anything'. You notice her mood. What do you do, and how do you use the sommelier's creative skill here?
options: Choose a wine with a story that fits the moment — a mineral natural wine from a small producer by the sea, perhaps — and present it briefly: 'This comes from a family that has farmed on the Atlantic coast for three generations. Something calm and clean.' Then read whether she wants more contact
Ask her in detail about her evening and her life
Offer the most expensive wine to make up for it
Pour from the nearest open bottle and leave her in peace
somm-e7.explanation: Herdenstam shows that the sommelier's craft includes reading situations and social skill. The creative grip is about making an experience that meets the guest where she is. A short story in the right tone is an aesthetic choice, not just a product presentation.

somm-dg1.prompt: You are leading a Double-Grip Analysis session with your sommelier team before a tasting menu at Ekbacken. You hand out paper and ask everyone to taste a Burgundy in silence — without the WSET protocol. Your first question is not 'What do you find in the glass?' What is the right opening question in the analogical tasting of Double-Grip Analysis? (Crichton-Fock & Spence, 2024)
options: 'Which grape is this most likely?'
'Describe the nose in WSET terms'
'Rate the intensity of the acidity on a scale of 1–9'
'What is awakened in you when your senses meet the wine?' — an autobiographical flow, without an analytical filter
somm-dg1.explanation: Double-Grip Analysis has two parallel tastings: analytical (deductive — what do I find in the glass?) and analogical (inductive — what is awakened in me?). The analogical one starts with autobiographical tasting, where personal smell memories and associations flow freely without ready-made templates. Groups in the study reached 8 shared attributes in both categories and created analogue wines that were rated higher than commercial equivalents.

somm-dg2.prompt: In a dialogue seminar (Herdenstam et al., 2018) a sommelier shares an autobiographical tasting: 'It's summer, tall grass, my grandmother's garden, the strawberry cake has stood too long in the sun...' A colleague cuts in: 'That's not a wine description — it's a fairy tale.' Why is the colleague's objection wrong from the point of view of phronesis?
options: Autobiographical descriptions are teaching exercises, not professional tools
The colleague is right — wine descriptions should be objective and analytical
Analogies and autobiographical memories carry knowledge that is harder to measure but easier to understand: they capture the character of the whole, which isolated analytical attributes cannot
The description is only useful if the sommelier and guest share exactly the same cultural background
somm-dg2.explanation: Herdenstam (2011, 2018, 2020): analogies and autobiographical stories are legitimate carriers of knowledge — 'lower measurability but high power of understanding' — and they capture the shape of the wine. 'Breaking the Silence' (2020) shows that analogical training actually increases the consistency of judgements and widens the shared vocabulary from 3 to 8 categories.

somm-cc1.prompt: Crichton-Fock, Spence & Pettersson (2023, Frontiers in Psychology) studied 329 wine consumers and crossmodal communication. The team at Nocturne discusses how to use the findings when talking to guests. Which finding matters most for a sommelier who wants to communicate the range more effectively?
options: Consumers prefer purely analytical terms — grapes and acidity levels

Visual communication through shapes and colours ranked highest (54 %), and 91 % were positive to buying wine on sensory information alone: consumers are more open to crossmodal communication than the trade assumes
Sound (music) was the most popular alternative form of communication
Consumers want no alternative communication — price and origin are enough
somm-cc1.explanation: Crichton-Fock et al. (2023): 91 % were positive to buying wine on sensory information alone. Shapes and colours (54 %), taste (45 %) and smell (38 %) dominated. A sommelier who uses crossmodal communication — shapes, analogies, storytelling — meets consumers' actual preferences better and can reduce waste of wines with an unconventional profile.

somm-bs1.prompt: In 'Breaking the Silence' (Herdenstam et al., 2020), dialogue seminars built on classic literature — Proust, Faulkner, Woolf, Joyce — were used to stimulate analogical thinking in sommeliers. Your colleague asks why fiction is used in wine-tasting training. What was the scientific reason for using modernist literary extracts in the training?
options: Modernist texts stimulate analogical and associative thinking: they encourage capturing the whole and the progression of an experience rather than analysing parts, which is exactly what phronesis asks for in tasting
The literature distracted the sommeliers from technical terms, which was unwanted
It was an arbitrary method with no particular teaching purpose
The literature taught the sommeliers new wine vocabulary directly
somm-bs1.explanation: Herdenstam et al. (2020): Proust, Faulkner, Woolf and Joyce were chosen for their avant-garde experimentation and their ability to capture sensory progression, shape and dynamics. The results: participants moved from analytical lists to narrative descriptions of the whole with stronger personal anchors, and their judgements became more consistent even though the number of attributes nearly doubled.

somm-hs1.prompt: Nocturne has an open kitchen — no doors, a toilet shared with guests, wine bottles visible all along the bar. Guests see the sommelier team rinsing glasses, tasting and sometimes taking a sip of water. A colleague is uncomfortable: 'We should have a clearer backstage.' What view do Hult & Scander (2024) support on dissolving frontstage and backstage?
options: Transparency only works in informal restaurants, never in fine dining
Guests who see backstage always lose trust in the service
The colleague is right — guests should never see backstage

A dissolved line between frontstage and backstage creates organic, transparent service that builds trust and fellowship with guests — provided the team can read the situation and show themselves 'as themselves' professionally
somm-hs1.explanation: Hult & Scander (2024): in contemporary restaurants, a dissolved frontstage and backstage creates 'fellowship' and transparency that strengthen the guest's experience. Goffman: new stages are created all the time. Organic service requires the team to master how they present themselves — being yourself is a professional skill, not a lack of formality.

somm-hs2.prompt: At Bergsmannen the team discusses how to sell a natural wine from an unusual producer in the Jura. The wine is technically a little unstable but has a wonderful story: the producer left an established estate after a conflict and started out alone. The sommelier tells the guest the story — not the grape. Which concept from Hult & Scander (2024) best explains why the producer's personal story can sell better than the wine's sensory profile?
options: The story is irrelevant — guests want objective tasting notes
Guests always choose on price and origin, never on a story
The sommelier acts as a cultural intermediary: the winemaker's personality and story communicate taste symbolically. The guest buys the story and the identity, not just the drink in the glass
Technical faults in a wine can never be made up for with a story
somm-hs2.explanation: Hult & Scander (2024): in the study a wine with 'unstable' qualities is sold through the producer's personal story — the guests exclaim 'What a lovely story, we'll have it!' Taste is communicated symbolically, not analytically. The sommelier is a cultural intermediary whose ability to convey personality and authenticity matters as much as WSET knowledge.

somm-hs3.prompt: On a fully booked Saturday night at Bryggan, Sara and Maja work the dining room without speaking. Sara lays cutlery as Maja clears plates; Maja pours wine as Sara sets out new glasses. Their coordination is seamless. What craft skill makes this wordless teamwork possible? (Hult & Scander, 2024)
options: They have memorised a formal service script
Familiarity knowledge: a deep understanding of each other's way of working, and of the situation, lets them improvise like 'a choreographed dance' without words
They are friends, and that is all that matters
Their work is routine and needs no active skill
somm-hs3.explanation: Hult & Scander (2024) describe this as organic service: 'Without having communicated, one follows the other's work.' This is techne at its most refined — familiarity with a colleague's rhythm and reading of the situation that makes silent coordination possible. Herdenstam (2011) calls a similar phenomenon 'the silent science of the working palate'.

somm-hs4.prompt: Ekbacken is recruiting a new floor sommelier. Candidate A is technically perfect — correct, formal, flawless WSET knowledge. Candidate B's technique is a little more uneven, but B has a strong personality, deep taste preferences for natural wine and a lively way of talking about producers. Guests remember B's tables for a long time. What view do Hult & Scander (2024) support on what professionalism in the dining room requires today?
options: Today's restaurant culture needs a cultural intermediary whose self-presentation, taste and personality are part of the service skill: B's ability to embody authenticity and create memorable experiences is as valuable as formal technique
Personality and technique are always equal — choose on salary
B's style only works in hipster restaurants, never in fine dining
Candidate A is always best — technique beats everything
somm-hs4.explanation: Hult & Scander (2024): 'It's not only the waiter who needs to seem genuine; it's the whole restaurant's personality.' Professionalism in the dining room today is about being authentically yourself, not playing a role. The sommelier's identity and taste are a resource, not a problem — provided they are combined with basic craft skill.

somm-hs5.prompt: Qvarnen is being renovated. The team discusses the new interior: polished surfaces and a black-and-white look, or natural materials, visible storage and simple craftsmanship? The owner asks what suits the restaurant's identity and guests. How does aesthetic framing relate to the sommelier team's skill? (Hult & Scander, 2024)
options: Aesthetics is only about good Instagram pictures
Polished surfaces always signal more skill than natural materials
The interior has nothing to do with the sommelier's professional skill
The restaurant's aesthetic framing — materials, lighting, how the bottles are displayed, how food is presented — extends the team's taste identity and tells guests directly what to expect
somm-hs5.explanation: Hult & Scander (2024): aesthetic framing is one of three core categories in how restaurants perform today. Interior, display and presentation communicate taste identity and set expectations. A wine list that reflects authenticity and craft production, displayed the right way in the room, is part of the sommelier's phronesis.

somm-sc1.prompt: A young sommelier at Bryggan has been invited to help at a winemaker's dinner hosted by a famous Burgundy producer in Gothenburg. A colleague asks: 'Is it really worth going? You'll learn more from books.' Why does taking part in such networks matter so much for a sommelier's development? (Scander et al., 2020)
options: Winemaker's dinners are for guests, not for sommeliers in training
Books are enough — practical experience adds nothing theory does not cover

Social capital turns into cultural capital: the right network gives access to legitimate taste and experience that cannot be learned from books — tasting the right wines in the right company becomes embodied as familiarity knowledge
It is only about prestige — the network gives no real knowledge
somm-sc1.explanation: Scander et al. (2020): social capital (knowing the right people) is converted into cultural capital (knowing what is good). The study shows that a sommelier's skill is largely shaped by who they spend time with, which experiences they gain access to, and how these become embodied as familiarity knowledge — not by formal education alone.

somm-sc2.prompt: At a theme night at Nocturne your team serves simple food: crisps, plain sandwiches and a few sides. The price is still 800 kronor a head. A guest raises an eyebrow. You explain the choice. Which reasoning best reflects Scander et al.'s finding about drink as a carrier of culture?
options: Simple food is a mistake — it never justifies the price, whatever the drink
The wine gives the food legitimacy: an outstanding wine can ennoble the humblest meal. The sommelier's skill lies in showing how the right drink raises the cultural and sensory value of the whole
The guest is right — simple food at a high price is always wrong
What matters is that the food is expensive, not the wine
somm-sc2.explanation: Scander et al. (2020): the sommeliers in the study stressed that 'a good wine goes with simple food — but not the other way round.' Drink carries culture and gives the pairing legitimacy. Pairing crisps with champagne expresses the sommelier's cultural capital, not a lack of skill.

somm-sc3.prompt: A new colleague at Järnvägshotellet asks how long it takes to become a competent sommelier. Your senior colleague answers: 'It depends on what you mean by competent.' Which two-step view of developing skill do Scander et al. (2020) describe?
options: Step 1: learn the basics of basic tastes, texture and pairing rules — fairly quickly. Step 2: build deep familiarity knowledge through long practical experience and the right social networks — which takes years
Step 1: read about every wine region. Step 2: memorise pairings
There is only one step — either you can pair food and drink or you cannot
Step 1: pass the WSET exam. Step 2: start working
somm-sc3.explanation: Scander et al. (2020): the basics (basic tastes, acidity, weight) are fairly easy to grasp but carry less cultural value. It is the second step — deep familiarity knowledge gained through years of practice and the right company — that makes up the sommelier's real cultural capital and professional identity.

somm-sc4.prompt: Bergsmannen is launching a new menu of decidedly 'lowbrow' dishes: hot dogs with trimmings, potato salad and classic falukorv sausage. The prices are high. Your team discusses whether the concept holds up from a professional sommelier's point of view. How do you justify the concept, drawing on Scander et al.'s research?
options: It only works if you tell the guests nothing about the ingredients
Simple ingredients always justify a lower price — no exceptions
It cannot be justified — the price always follows the quality of the ingredients

The sommelier's cultural capital means lowbrow food can be given legitimacy through the right drink. The concept requires a team skilled enough to choose and communicate wines that raise and transform the dishes' cultural status
somm-sc4.explanation: Scander et al. (2020): the study shows that lowbrow food — crisps and simple sausage included — gains legitimacy with the right drink. The sommelier's ability to communicate this transformation is the core of cultural capital. The concept requires high skill, not expensive ingredients.

somm-sc5.prompt: Lärkan is recruiting a new sommelier. Two candidates apply: A has WSET Level 3 and three years in a training restaurant. B has no formal training but has worked five years in well-known restaurants, entered sommelier competitions and has a wide professional network. Which way of judging competence is most in line with Scander et al.'s research?
options: B is always better — experience always beats training
A is always better — formal training is all that counts

B's informally gained social and cultural capital — practical experience, the right network, competition exposure — can be as valuable as formal merits, or more, depending on what the restaurant needs
The candidates are identical — experience and training always weigh the same
somm-sc5.explanation: Scander et al. (2020) show that a sommelier's skill is built from a combination of formal knowledge and social capital. Competitions, mentoring by leading sommeliers and professional networks build familiarity knowledge that is hard to replace with schooling alone — but not enough without basic analytical skill either.

options: Always play it safe — unusual pairings always damage the guests' trust

The sommelier's agency means the freedom and the responsibility to experiment with unorthodox pairings. With the right communication — the wine's origin, analogies for how the taste unfolds — the team can transform the guests' expectations and open up new experiences
Experimental pairings belong on theme nights only, never on the regular menu
The guest's preferences always decide — the sommelier should never challenge their comfort zone
somm-sc6.explanation: Scander et al. (2020): 'The individual sommelier's agency matters as much as structural conditions. Becoming part of the profession requires sociability, creativity and a willingness to experiment with sometimes odd pairings.' Communicating experimental choices professionally — with a story and knowledgeable guidance — is a sign of strong phronesis.
